He should have apologised today saying five of us were not enough, so I brought the sixth. And I know that as a most renounced professor of law, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen -- let's resume because that is a point of detail. Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and good afternoon. I believe if you check the transcript, Mr. Marcussen said there would be five in addition to himself and named all five of us. The crimes charged in Mostar and Nevesinje were part of the joint criminal enterprise. JCE members, including the accused, targeted the region and deployed forces under their control, while those implementing the JCE on the ground created or took control over local instruments of power. When the conflict reached Eastern Herzegovina, joint Serb forces, including Seseljevci, fought under JNA, TO, and VRS officers. Witnesses clearly and repeatedly identified members of those same joint Serb forces, including Seseljevci, as physical perpetrators of the crimes in the area. Since the crimes were part of the JCE and the perpetrators were part of Serb forces on the ground and subordinated to JCE members, the accused is responsible as a member of the JCE. To demonstrate, I will address three issues. I will first explain how JCE members, including the accused, targeted Eastern Herzegovina and created and deployed co-ordinated forces to establish Serb domination of the area. I will then describe the campaign of destruction and murder those forces carried out in Mostar. Finally, I will describe the campaign of destruction and murder which obliterated the non-Serb population of Nevesinje, their homes, their villages, and their cultural institutions. JCE members had targeted the Eastern Herzegovina region from the beginning of the conflict. The region was strategically important, and to control it, JCE members deployed their own forces to Eastern Herzegovina and established and supported forces based in the area. Control of Eastern Herzegovina supported three of the strategic goals of the Bosnian Serb leadership. Goal number one, separation of the Serbian people from the Muslim and Croat communities; goal number four, a border on the Neretva and Una Rivers; and goal number six, access to the Adriatic Sea via Herzegovina. Mostar itself also boasted a significant military infrastructure. On 16 September 1991, the Bosnian Serb leadership declared the SAO Herzegovina, the Srpska Autonomna Oblast of Herzegovina. This included Nevesinje. Just days later, the JNA's Uzice Corps deployed additional forces to the area and General Torbica held a meeting with local Serb leaders where he told them Serbia would fulfil its historical destiny and gain control of territory mirroring the accused's vision of Greater Serbia. The JNA and Serb police then distributed thousands of arms to the local Serb population. These arms were first used often in the combat in Croatia, but once conflict began in Bosnia, the same arms supported the implementation of the JCE in Eastern Herzegovina. As Yugoslavia began to split apart, the JNA, under JCE members Milosevic and Adzic, deployed forces under General Momcilo Perisic to the region in mass. The Red Berets, under JCE members Stanisic and Simatovic, established a training camp in nearby Trebinje for police special operations units and at least one special operations unit from the Trebinje police was deployed to the war in Croatia. And at the beginning of 1992, Serb leaders in Nevesinje established a Crisis Staff. By now, the patterns Mr. Mussemeyer had described were visible in Eastern Herzegovina. The Serb population had been armed and separate parallel Serb institutions had been created. As the Serb forces coalesced in Eastern Herzegovina, life began to change for non-Serb civilians. Members of Arsen Grahovac's Karadjordje unit told non-Serbs they would end up in mass graves if they did not leave Nevesinje. And for non-Serbs like Witness Kujan, life in Nevesinje became "like living in a prison camp." And that's from Exhibit P524, page 4. The accused himself made an enormous contribution to the campaign in Eastern Herzegovina. He had begun targeting the region in early 1991, meeting with Chetnik commanders and establishing co-operation with local Serb leaders, including Karadjordje unit commander Grahovac and local SDS leader Bozidar Vucurevic. The accused went to the region in fall 1991, visiting Nevesinje, Gacko, Trebinje, and Bileca, as well as travelling to the ethnically-cleansed town of Konavle, Croatia, with Vucurevic. Your Honours can see this, for instance, in Exhibits P1162 and P1394. After the accused visited, Seseljevci formed units which went to fight in Croatia, and Croats in the region discussed forming their own volunteer units in response for defence. The accused's targeting of Eastern Herzegovina and co-operation with local leaders is set out in, for instance, Exhibits P163, P524, P880, P881, and P989, as well as the exhibits I mentioned earlier. As Serb take-overs began in BiH, the accused publicly announced he would visit Eastern Herzegovina again, in Exhibits P685 and P1296. When he arrived, he met with Vucurevic and Grahovac. This visit is discussed in Exhibit P524. Like other local Serb leaders across BiH and Croatia, Vucurevic asked the accused for additional manpower to support Serb forces. The accused's Vojvoda Vakic describes this in "Velika Srbija" in Exhibit P55. And on 30 March 1992, the accused gave a press conference in Trebinje, just south of Nevesinje. He called upon Bosnian Serbs to act through their own authorities in their territories to complete what he called the liberation of their territories: "... with the help of the Territorial Defence and Serbian volunteers whom we can send whenever this is necessary. We will start sending these volunteers to Herzegovina in the very near future." That's from Exhibit P1109, page 1. In his brief, the accused attacks Witness Kujan for testifying that the accused was present in Nevesinje in early 1992. But as this evidence shows, the accused did visit Eastern Herzegovina in March 1992, where he called for further conflict and promised to send Seseljevci to the region. When he returned to Belgrade, the accused called for Serb forces to seize "the whole Neretva River valley." That's from Exhibit P1262, page 14. As the accused had promised and as he did throughout the conflict, he then contributed his Seseljevci to the Serb forces in Eastern Herzegovina. On 8 April 1992, the Ministry for Serbs Outside Serbia requested three buses to transport what they called refugees from Belgrade to areas of Eastern Herzegovina, including Nevesinje. That's Exhibit P1070. And war chief staff -- sorry, War Staff Chief Ljubisa Petkovic explained in his evidence that this was merely a ruse to conceal the buses' real purpose: Transporting Seseljevci to the front lines. And that's in Exhibit C16, page 74. The accused deployed hundreds of other Seseljevci to Eastern Herzegovina, where five of his Vojvodas led Seseljevci into battle. The Trial Chamber is referred to Exhibits P54, P55, P843, P846, P889, P1002, and P1311, where the accused and his Seseljevci discuss this deployment themselves. Official records of Serb forces and both Serb and Bosnian police show Seseljevci in the region in, for instance, Exhibits P29, P891, P1008, and P1162. Details about the Seseljevci who were deployed to Eastern Herzegovina are set out in paragraphs 264 through 271 of the Prosecution's closing brief. The accused's own war-time statements corroborate this evidence and show his men remained in Eastern Herzegovina at the time of the crimes charged in his indictment. Exhibit P218, in which the accused declared many of his men to be Vojvodas, shows that Vojvoda Tripkovic was still fighting in Mostar on 14 June 1992, and that Vojvoda Baret remained in the area until 31 July 1992, after the massacres at Uborak and Sutina, which I will discuss in due course. Other Seseljevci remained in nearby Eastern Herzegovina, easily close enough to Mostar and Nevesinje to fight and commit crimes there, until well after the crimes charged in the indictment had been committed. In another order declaring his men to be Vojvodas, the accused stated in Exhibit P217 that Vojvoda Vakic fought in Herzegovina in both May and June of 1992, that Vojvoda Radovan Radovic fought in the Neretva valley and Nevesinje in both 1992 and 1993, and that Vojvoda Nedjeljko Vidjakovic also commanded a Seseljevci unit from Trebinje which fought in the region. And Exhibits C10 and P891 confirm that large groups of Seseljevci were in Eastern Herzegovina until months after the crimes charged in this case. Credible witness identifications place these Seseljevci among the perpetrators of crimes. Witnesses Dabic, VS-1067, and Tot were members of Serb forces. Consequently, they were well positioned to correctly identify a particular fighting force's affiliation, whether to one Serb force or another. Victim witnesses VS-1022, Bilic, and Karisik were detained for at least several days and mistreated and had the opportunity to learn identifying information about their tormentors. And indeed, civilians in Eastern Herzegovina knew to fear the Seseljevci. As Witness Stoparic testified, when his Seseljevci unit went through villages, non-Serb civilians would flee. Despite the Seseljevci's crimes, when forces were needed in Eastern Herzegovina, even in 1993, Slobodan Milosevic continued to personally call on the accused, and the accused provided thousands of additional volunteers. He himself declared that he sent Seseljevci to areas right near Mostar at Milosevic's behest, long after he now claims his Seseljevci had left the region. That's in Exhibit P644, page 17. As in Vukovar and elsewhere, the accused has attempted to downplay his contribution to the campaign in Eastern Herzegovina now that he is faced with international justice. He argues that Seseljevci left the Mostar area around 19 May 1992, before the massacres at Uborak and Sutina, and that no significant number of Seseljevci were present in Nevesinje. The evidence I have summarised proves beyond a reasonable doubt that Seseljevci, in fact, remained in and around Mostar and Nevesinje while crimes were committed. The accused's arguments in this respect are unconvincing. First, he asserts that the Seseljevci must have withdrawn from Mostar by 25 May 1992 because Vojvoda Ba ret was in Podgorica, Montenegro, with the accused on that date. This assertion addresses only one of the hundreds of Seseljevci in the Mostar area at the time, and another Vojvoda, Vakic, often travelled from Eastern Herzegovina to Podgorica for supplies, as he told "Velika Srbija" in Exhibit P54. Consequently, even if Baret were in Podgorica with the accused on 25 May, it would not suggest that Seseljevci were no longer in Mostar at the time. Next, the accused attempts to cast doubt on the identifications of his men. He asserts that Witnesses Karisik, Bilic, and VS-1051 did not mention the accused or his Seseljevci in their initial statements to local authorities. Victim witnesses Karisik and VS-1051 were cross-examined as to why they had not identified the Seseljevci who participated in the crimes against them when they first gave statements to local authorities. VS-1051 explained that the witness was still traumatised when the statement was given and Karisik stood by his identification of Seseljevci under cross-examination. Regarding Witness Bilic, the accused's claim that the witness did not identify Seseljevci is unsupported by any evidence in the record and, moreover, was not raised on cross-examination in violation of Rule 90(H)(ii) and should not be considered. The accused further argues that Witnesses Dabic, VS-1022, and VS-1067 offered only hearsay testimony about Seseljevci. Those witnesses' evidence is admissible before this Tribunal and well corroborated. In this regard, the Chamber should consider particularly Exhibits P887, P889, P891, and P1162, along, of course, with the witnesses' own evidence. The accused also asserts that Witnesses Kujan and VS-1068 were mistaken in identifying his men as perpetrators, but provides no support for this proposition. And he ignores Witness Zoran Tot, his own volunteer, who gave evidence that Seseljevci participated in crimes including the wanton destruction of Mostar. Finally, the accused denies witness evidence that his Seseljevci were present at Boracko Jezero, which I will come to later, even though Vojvoda Vakic informed the Serbian Assembly in 1993 that a Seseljevci commander had, in fact, been killed in Boracko Jezero. And that's in Exhibit P889, page 19. Dispute the accused's denials, it is clear that he and his Seseljevci made a significant and substantial contribution to the persecutorial campaign in Eastern Herzegovina and to the field of operations in which the crimes were committed. As I will next explain, the accused is also linked to the combined Serb forces in Eastern Herzegovina by his contribution to their campaign. These combined Serb forces were directly linked to JCE members including the accused. As these slides show, all Serb forces in Eastern Herzegovina were subordinated to JCE members. Thus, the JCE members, including the accused, are jointly responsible for their crimes. As this first slide reflects, Serb forces in Eastern Herzegovina were initially subordinated to the JNA under General Perisic, which was subordinated to JCE members Blagoje Adzic and Slobodan Milosevic. After the JNA withdrew, Serb forces in the area were led by the VRS Herzegovina Corps, which was under the control of JCE members Ratko Mladic and Radovan Karadzic. Seseljevci in the region were subordinated to the official Serb armies, the accused himself discusses this in his Milosevic testimony and in Exhibit P1002, as were Savic and his police, the Red Berets, the Karadjordje unit, and local Serb forces such as the TO. When members of those forces committed crimes within the common purpose of the JCE, those crimes were attributable to the JNA or VRS commands and thus linked to Milosevic, Karadzic, Adzic, Mladic, and the other JCE members including the accused. As the second slide will reflect, many of the Serb forces in Eastern Herzegovina were also part of hierarchical structures linked to other JCE members. As reflected here, Seseljevci were members of a hierarchical structure headed by the accused. Savic and his police as well as the local Serb TO were part of structures headed by JCE member Radovan Karadzic. The Red Berets were part of a structure headed by JCE members Stanisic and Simatovic. Relevant evidence is set forth on the slide, including Exhibits P410 and P1033 and adjudicated fact 193 from this Chamber's 10 December 2007 decision. Relevant evidence is also summarised in the section of our closing brief discussing the structure of the accused's political and paramilitary organisations. Crimes committed by members of these forces also link to the JCE members, including the accused, through the JCE members atop those hierarchical structures. The accused offers two arguments relevant to the linkage between Serb forces and JCE members in his brief. First, he argues that this Tribunal has not previously convicted a commander or a physical perpetrator for the crimes in Mostar, and he thus cannot be held responsible as a member of the JCE. This is mistaken. There is no legal requirement that a physical or intermediate perpetrator must have been convicted for JCE liability to attach. Second, the accused argues that he cannot be held responsible for the crimes in Eastern Herzegovina because the perpetrators were local Serbs; this is mistaken. What the evidence shows is that members of Serb forces in Eastern Herzegovina, including local Serbs who fought in those forces, are linked to JCE members in two ways. They are dually linked to the JNA or VRS and to the JCE members leading their own hierarchical structures. The JCE members are thus jointly criminally responsible for crimes committed by members of Serb forces in the region, no matter to which specific force a specific perpetrator belonged. For that principle, this Chamber can refer to, for instance, the Brdjanin appeal judgement, paragraphs 409 and 413. With the linkage between the accused and the various Serb forces in Eastern Herzegovina in mind, I will turn to the conflict and crimes in Mostar. Conflict began in BiH at the end of March 1992. On 2 April, the accused called for Serb forces to "seize the entire Neretva valley" and ensure "a link between Eastern Herzegovina, Romanija, and Ozren." That's from Exhibit P1262, pages 14 and 15. Days later, conflict engulfed Mostar. The SDS ordered Serbs to leave and Serb forces shelled the city ruthlessly. Civilians were killed, including a Croat beaten and murdered by Seseljevci and JNA troops. Seseljevci arrived in nearby Buna and Bjelusine from whence they destroyed and looted villages such as Topla. One of the perpetrators was a Seseljevac named Vranjanac. Vranjanac identified himself as a Seseljevac to other members of Serb forces, and this is corroborated by Exhibits P891 and P1051. The accused's attempt to distance himself from Vranjanac should be rejected. By the end of May, the east bank of the Neretva River had been ethnically cleansed of non-Serbs. In Mostar, non-Serb civilians fled to shelters to escape JNA shelling. Witnesses Bilic, Karisik, and VS-1068 described how Serb forces, including Seseljevci, held civilians prisoner in the Zalik shelter and forced civilians to labour while exposed to gun-fire and physical assault. They described how detainees were sometimes taken to the JNA north camp and mistreated and at least one detainee never returned. Serb fighters would tell detainees stories about murdering non-Serbs, and they would tell them the area would one day all be part of Greater Serbia, and they so terrorised the detainees that one witness testified: "You couldn't even hear very well for all of the crying and screaming in the shelter." The indiscriminate and disproportionate shelling of non-military structures in Mostar escalated just before the JNA withdrew from the city. As Exhibits P843 and P846 describe, General Perisic ordered Serb forces including Seseljevci to shell Mostar with no specific targets. Civilians who fled the shelling were mopped up under Perisic's orders. And here I'd refer Your Honours particularly to the evidence of Witness Tot, particularly in Exhibit P843, paragraphs 49 and 50. JCE member Ratko Mladic's notes reveal his awareness that Perisic was "destroying Mostar." That's in Exhibit P1344 at page 7. And the accused's Vojvoda Oliver Baret was present in JNA headquarters during the bombing, co-ordinating between the JNA and the Seseljevci in Mostar. And as Riedlmayer's report and the associated exhibits demonstrate, Serb forces devastated and destroyed non-Serb religious and cultural sites throughout Mostar during this campaign. Earlier in the proceedings, the accused attempted to justify the destruction of Mostar, by stating that the west bank of the Neretva River was in the hands of Croatian forces and the JNA was simply resisting them. Essentially, he argues Serb forces' wanton destruction was justified and defensive. This is incorrect. First, the wanton and indiscriminate shelling of a civilian population can hardly be qualified as defensive. Second, this Tribunal's jurisprudence is quite clear that combatants and their leaders may not shield their violations of international humanitarian law behind an allegedly defensive operation. The critical consideration for the accused's liability is that members of Serb forces for whose crimes he is culpable violated international humanitarian law in destroying Mostar, not his assertion that some of Mostar's territory was under Croatian control when they did so. For that principle, I would refer Your Honours to paragraphs 268 of the Martic appeal judgement and paragraph 812 of the Kordic and Cerkez appeal judgement. Conflict in the Mostar area --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a very important correction. The interpreter is saying "Mladic" case, but it's, in fact, the Martic case. There is still no judgement in the Mladic case. You should avoid confusing the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. The English transcript reads "Martic." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Conflict in the Mostar area continued after the JNA shelled and devastated the city and then turned over its weapons to the VRS and officially withdrew from BiH. When Serb forces suffered casualties in a nearby operation, Zdravko Kandic, the Mostar TO commander who had become a battalion commander in the VRS, ordered Serb forces to round up non-Serbs from East Mostar. Those Serb forces detained, abused, and eventually massacred non-Serbs in three nearby locations: Vrapcici stadium, Uborak junkyard, and Sutina cemetery. We are now showing Exhibit P488, which you can see on your screens. That exhibit shows the Zalik shelter, the JNA north camp, and Vrapcici, Uborak, and Sutina. In the bottom left-hand corner you can see north camp and the Zalik shelter and you can see how a single main road from the shelter leads to Sutina, Vrapcici, and finally Uborak. Serb forces at Kandic's direction rounded up Witness Karisik and other non-Serbs and took them to Sutina cemetery and then to Vrapcici stadium. Eventually, 90 people were held in the stadium in horrible conditions, including women and children. Karisik ate and drank only once in six days. He expected to die. Eventually, Karisik and others were taken out in a van and the others were murdered by the side of the road. Serb forces, including Seseljevci, took other non-Serbs to Uborak junkyard and murdered them as well. Karisik was instead taken back to Sutina where he was beaten but eventually escaped. Chetniks rounded up other non-Serbs at a shelter in Zalik. They were taken to the Sutina cemetery, brutally abused, then taken outside and murdered. Some were forced to assist in dumping murder victims in a mass grave. The massacres at Uborak and Sutina followed a round-up of civilians directly ordered by VRS commander Zdravko Kandic and carried out by subordinate Serb forces. The organised nature of the massacre is evident. For instance, a member of the Serb forces stated when Karisik's group arrived at Sutina: "They're not for here. Take them to Vrapcici." And that's from T8776. Kandic was subordinated to the Bosnian Serb leadership, including VRS commander Mladic. Witnesses identified perpetrators carrying out his operation from various Serb forces, including Seseljevci and their local collaborators. All the perpetrators were subordinated to Kandic, carrying out his orders and consequently linked to the VRS and the Bosnian Serb leadership, and through them linked to the other JCE members, including the accused. The JCE members also implemented their common purpose in Nevesinje. In preparation, Serb leaders armed the local Serb population, removed non-Serbs from local police forces, and replaced the mayor of Nevesinje. Serb forces also set up check-points which deprived Nevesinje Muslims of freedom of movement. These were often manned by Seseljevci, including a man named Kinez, as well as police and members of the Karadjordje unit. Some Serb fighters at check-points can be seen in Exhibit P887, stating that they only recognised the authority of the accused and his fellow JCE member Milan Martic. As a note, some of the evidence regarding check-points originates from Witness Dabic. This witness' credibility is discussed in the argumentative annex to our closing brief, and I will not repeat this discussion every time we rely on his evidence. Regarding Seseljevci's presence at check-points, however, I point out that the witness's evidence is corroborated by official documentation and video evidence. The persecutory campaign in Nevesinje accelerated after conflict started in BiH and reached nearby Mostar. Many Serbs who left Mostar at SDS orders went to Nevesinje and drove Nevesinje Muslims out of their homes. Non-Serbs were killed and others fled to the woods and then out of the municipality entirely to save their lives. These non-Serbs suffered forcible transfer, as is clear in paragraphs 279 through 281 of the Stakic appeal judgement. Earlier in these proceedings the accused asked Your Honours how could they, meaning Serb forces, attack Nevesinje when 90 per cent of its population was Serb anyway ? The actual number was 74 per cent according to the census. JCE members in the Bosnian Serb leadership did not exclude Serb majority municipalities from their persecutory campaign. Instead, they had established specific instructions for targeting Serb majority municipalities, Variant A. As you can see in Exhibit P524, page 5, the same steps described in Variant A were implemented in Nevesinje. And in June 1992, Serb forces implementing the JCE in Nevesinje decided that it was not enough for Nevesinje to be a Serb-majority municipality. It would be made pure Serbian, just the way DB official Mihalj Kertes had described the Drina River valley in Eastern Bosnia. Serb fighters were explicitly ordered to ethnically cleanse Nevesinje municipality. Their operational orders were to "burn down ... destroy everything ... make the villages and people disappear." And that's from Exhibit P880, page 31. As Witness Kujan and others described, Serb forces in Nevesinje carried out those orders with chilling completeness. Beginning in the second week of June, Serb forces under the VRS would shell villages, then enter, loot and burn down homes, massacre any remaining non-Serb civilians, and finally burn down the entire village. By the end of June, the entire non-Serb population had fled or been massacred. Their villages had been destroyed and their holy sites had been either destroyed or seriously damaged. Witness Kujan described the Serb forces' campaign in terms that mirrored their orders, as you will see in this slide show. This first slide shows the orders given to Serb forces in Nevesinje: Burn down, destroy everything, make the villages and the people disappear. One of the most visible things to disappear was non-Serbs' holy and sacred places. Before the war, Nevesinje had one Catholic church, one Orthodox church, and three mosques. Today, only the Orthodox church remains. The other religious buildings have been levelled and turned into parking-lots. You can see the old Nevesinje Catholic church which was completely destroyed by Seseljevci under Vranjanac on this slide. The next slide shows Witness Kujan's description of the JCE campaign. After describing the destruction of non-Serb religious institutions, he explains that Serb forces "wanted to destroy everything that wasn't Serbian, and they did just that." That's from Exhibit P524, page 2. The third slide discusses the pattern of attacks. Witness Kujan stated: "The pattern of these attacks I witnessed was the same. There would be shelling first, then entering the villages, then burning down of some houses. The village would be cleared of people and all movable property would be stolen from inside and outside the homes. Cars and any equipment would be taken away and then the whole village would be burnt down." That's from Exhibit P524, page 6. And I would refer Your Honours for comparison to the description of Serb forces' tactics during their campaign in Croatia in Exhibit P412. The final slide from Exhibit P524, page 8, shows the consequences of the JCE campaign, non-Serbs fled from Nevesinje. And by 26 June 1992, Nevesinje had been "totally ethnically cleansed of its non-Serb population." The non-Serb villages and people had quite literally disappeared from Nevesinje municipality. As it already had in Vukovar, Zvornik, Greater Sarajevo, and Mostar, the Serb forces' campaign in Nevesinje led to massacres and the torture and cruel treatment of detained persons. Evidence can be found in, among others, Exhibits P483, P487, P523, P524, P525, P880, P881, and P1052. One group of Muslim civilians attempting to flee from the Serb forces' campaign was caught hiding in the woods near Teleca Lastva. They were detained, interrogated, and tortured, and some of the women were raped or sexually abused. Seven of the prisoners were taken away by Serb forces, including Seseljevci, and never seen alive again. The survivors were ordered to clean up the blood left over from prisoners being tortured. But the crimes in Eastern Herzegovina and perhaps best -- and indeed, in Bosnia as a whole, are perhaps best represented by the stories of Fadila and Mirsada Mahinic. Relevant evidence about the crimes against their group of civilians is set forth in paragraphs 473 to 478 of the Prosecution's closing brief. What that evidence shows is this: In late June 1992, a group of Muslim civilians fled the villages of Presjeka and Kljuna under heavy shelling. Some left behind their elderly parents who knew they would be murdered but stayed behind to avoid slowing down their families and making their escape more difficult. Those who stayed were, indeed, murdered and their bodies were not even identified until 1998. The group that left, including the Mahinics, were captured by Serb forces and held until VRS officer Zdravko Kandic arrived. While they were held, Serb forces and local Serbs taunted the group, saying: "Fuck your balija mothers. We'll kill you, we'll slaughter you." And told one woman: "Shut up, you balija, balinka. You are guilty of being a Muslim." After Kandic arrived and spoke to their captors, the men in the group were taken away and killed in the Dubravica pit. The women and children, including Habib and Ferida Sipkovic and their 7-day-old baby, were held in the basement of the Kilavci heating plant with no light and no food or water. They were abused by members of the Serb forces, one of whom identified the perpetrators as including Seseljevci. The Mahinics and a few other women were taken away to Boracko Jezero while the other members of their group were murdered, including the baby who the evidence shows had not even lived long enough to have a name. Eleven other victims named Mahinic were killed. When Serb forces were selecting women to take to Boracko Jezero, one Serb fighter looked at the new mother and said: "You see, she's just had a baby ... she's no use to us. Who's going to fuck with her?" The women who were taken away could have had no doubt what their captors intended. And a Serb named Petar Divjakovic then took the selected women towards the motel at Boracko Jezero, where Chetniks told them they would be raped. Women in the group were, indeed, raped and detainees were viciously beaten. Almost ten years later the Mahinics' bodies were found in a nearby mass grave. The Mahinics' story encompasses all of the counts charged in Nevesinje municipality. The villages of members of their group were wantonly destroyed, leaving them no choice but to flee and constituting forcible transfer. When they were captured, the Serb forces tortured, raped, cruelly treated, and massacred members of their group. And they themselves were murdered. The repeated ethnic slurs hurled at them and their fellow Muslims reveal that the perpetrators of these crimes committed the crimes with the discriminatory intent characteristic of persecution. And perpetrators identified as Seseljevci participated in the crimes. These crimes and the others in Mostar and Nevesinje were an integral part of the common plan to ethnically cleanse Serb-targeted territories throughout BiH of their non-Serb populations and to create Serb-controlled areas. Serb forces including Seseljevci followed their orders to make non-Serb villages and people disappear through wanton destruction, forcible transfer, and persecution. Non-Serbs who were tragically captured by Serb forces, like the Mahinics and several of the witnesses in this case, were brutalised, tortured, and murdered in large numbers. Next, having discussed the crimes in Mostar and Nevesinje, Ms. Biersay will next discuss how, as non-Serbs began to flee Nevesinje in May of 1992, the accused himself personally committed persecution and forcible transfer against the non-Serbs of Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor. As Mrs. Biersay is going to take the floor, we are going to have a break now, a 20-minute break and we shall resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. You may proceed, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before starting, I wanted to tell the Trial Chamber that I provided to the Chamber and to the accused a sheet that associates the names of three witnesses with a letter of the alphabet and this is just to ensure that the identities of witnesses are not disclosed when I address nonpublic information. I may not use all the names, but I understand that the Trial Chamber would prefer not to go in and out of private session. So this is my attempt to try to prevent doing that. Hopefully I can make it work. Your Honours, the accused committed crimes in Croatia. He committed crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And he also committed crimes in Serbia. In this case, he gave a speech in the village of Hrtkovci on May 6, 1992. That speech ignited the flames of ethnic hatred and forever changed the face of that village. He accomplished exactly what he set out to do: To force Croats out of the village and out of Serbia. Before Yugoslavia started breaking apart, the village of Hrtkovci in Vojvodina, Serbia, was ethnically diverse. It had a Croat majority, as well as Hungarians and Serbs. Witnesses described that there were many mixed marriages between Serbs and Croats or Hungarians. And the people of different ethnicities, they lived together in peace and in harmony. That tranquility began to change, slowly at first, as the village was infected by the violent inter-ethnic conflict in neighbouring Croatia and then in BiH as more and more refugees from -- Serb refugees came into Vojvodina looking for safety and places to live. After the accused delivered his hate speech on 6 May 1992, the changes that had begun slowly in Hrtkovci exploded into ethnic tension and fear. The accused personally brought that tension and fear to the people of Hrtkovci with his hatred. He personally made Croats so afraid that many fled the village soon after. He personally encouraged Serb refugees in Hrtkovci to participate in his persecution campaign against Croats. As highlighted in paragraphs 561 and 562 of the Prosecution's closing brief, the evidence shows beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused physically committed persecution through the hate speech because of what he said, who he was, and the context of war in which he made the speech. He targeted Hrtkovci as the place for the May 6 SRS rally because Hrtkovci was majority Croat and was considered "Ustasha" territory during World War II. And not only did he target Hrtkovci as a place for this rally, he targeted the date. He targeted May 6 as the day for the SRS rally in Hrtkovci because it was St. George's Day, a very important Serb holiday. So he chose to spend a significant Serb holiday in a Croat majority village, an event that was advertised with posters and announced on Radio Ruma, transcript page 10337. On the day of the accused's hate speech, he and the SRS set the stage for maximum impact. They purposely filled Hrtkovci with an intimidating atmosphere. Ethnically divisive and intimidating Chetnik music played from a loudspeaker. A large group of armed men wearing black World War II-era Chetnik uniforms arrived and spread throughout the town. A much larger crowd of Serb refugees was present at the rally site. They had all come to see and hear the accused. And there are also some local Croats there as well. This is described at transcript page 10335 and in Exhibits P329 and 1329. The security provided for the rally far surpassed that of any electoral campaign. In addition to the armed Chetnik men, there was a policeman with an automatic rifle in the street at every 100 metres. The level of security provided for the rally was so intense, it reminded Witness Ejic of the times when Tito passed through. A member of the accused's security detail carried what appeared to be a bayonet and stood by the stage. It was clear, clear that the objective was to "create fear, a different psychological atmosphere among the local population." Transcript pages 10335, 10337 to 10338, and 10489. A list of prominent Croats in Hrtkovci was read to the crowd. The accused admits in Exhibit P31, pages 1304 to 1305, that a member of the SRS party standing next to him read out the list. And those Croats were labelled as disloyal. During his speech, the accused repeated his rhetoric of hatred and division and pounded his chest. He called for a Greater Serbia. He denigrated Croats of Hrtkovci as Ustasha. He labelled them disloyal enemies of the Serbian people. He accused some Croats as being in the "Ustasha National Guard", branded their parents as disloyal and as having no place in Hrtkovci. He called for Croats to be forced out of Hrtkovci. He shouted: "Let them go to their homeland." He accused Tudjman of driving Serbs from Croatia. And he promised Serb refugees they could move into the Croat houses in Hrtkovci. He encouraged every Serb family of refugees to knock on a Croat door and give its inhabitants an address in a Croatian place outside of Serbia. He delivered an ultimatum to Hrtkovci Croats: Move to Croatia or be placed on buses and be sent to the border, saying: "There will be enough buses. We will drive them to the border of Serb territory and they can walk on from there." And that's in Exhibit P547 at page 4. He instructed "Serbs from Hrtkovci and other villages" to "promptly get rid of the remaining Croats." He promised Serbs that they would overcome economic and social crisis by getting rid of the remaining Croats, and he threatened Croats that "they would have nowhere to return to." Very similar language that he used with respect to the cleansed town of Osijek that I described to the Trial Chamber previously. And what did the crowd do? The crowd applauded and shouted "Ustasha out ... this is Serbia." As addressed in the Prosecution closing brief at paragraphs 559 and 562, the accused's May 6 speech constitutes persecution. In his speech, the accused invoked a litany of the same hateful denigration that he used to justify the commission of crimes to achieve the common criminal purpose in Croatia and in BiH. In a book published after he was indicted in this case, the accused produced a partial transcript of that May 6 speech. Even though it is a partial transcript, it fully establishes the accused's intent to persecute Croats through his hate speech, especially given the context in which the speech was given, namely, the raging inter-ethnic conflict in Croatia and in BiH. When the accused finished his May 6th hate speech, he had personally committed the crime of persecution. And despite what he claims, his speech in Hrtkovci was not an innocent election promise. As set out in the Nahimana appeals judgement, especially in paragraph 771, there is no legal protection for hate speech based on conditional language. This accused delivered a speech filled with ethnic hatred and fear-mongering. He exploited his status and authority to deliberately fuel the tension between local Croats and Serb refugees. He exploited the ongoing violence in Croatia that made both Croats and Serbs frightened. By so doing, he breached the cloak that protects free speech and transformed his hate speech into a crime in and of itself; and for that, he is criminally responsible. His speech violated the Croats' right to dignity and security. The Croats in Hrtkovci who heard his words or heard about them knew that he was not making empty threats. They knew the accused was an influential elected official who publicly flaunted his quasi-military authority inside and outside of Serbia. They knew about the crimes committed by Seseljevci. They knew the accused influenced and controlled Seseljevci, and he was synonymous with his Seseljevci, and they were notorious for their participation in crimes committed in Croatia. And I'd refer to transcript 1545 as well as 15411 and 15412. Immediately after his speech, many Croats began preparing to leave Hrtkovci, showing they felt denigrated and threatened, just as the accused intended. By August 1992, the Serb leadership of the village changed the name of Hrtkovci to Srbislavci to reflect that Serbs were now the majority. That's only three months after the accused's May 6 speech. Even the signposts into and out of the village were changed to Srbislavci. Transcript pages 10382 to 10383 as well as Exhibit P549. But the accused had begun targeting non-Serbs in Vojvodina and Hrtkovci as early as September 1991 during the war in Croatia. And I'm now citing the evidence of Witness A on your sheet. As described in Exhibits P1112, pages 5 to 6; P1129, pages 26 to 28, 161 to 163, the accused gave instructions in September of 1991 for how this persecution campaign should be carried out in Hrtkovci: Dismissing non-Serbs from government jobs, threatening non-Serbs through intimidating telephone calls, attacking non-Serbs, attacking their homes, marking non-Serb houses, throwing grenades, and breaking windows. So at the same time he was giving instructions for the persecution campaign against Hrtkovci's Croats in 1991, the accused was also denigrating Croats in Croatia. Serb forces, including Seseljevci, implemented a brutal campaign of persecution against Croats in targeted areas of Croatia. And his persecutorial speeches and the campaign itself were reported throughout Serbia. And it's important to consider what the Croats in Serbia were seeing. Throughout Croatia, JNA tanks rolled, Croat towns shelled, Croats expelled, Croats killed. Croatia was being cleansed of Croats and the accused wanted to cleanse Serbia of its Croats. But this did not happen in 1991 or in the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The accused -- before the May 6 hate speech, it's true that two or three Croat families did leave, and I'd refer the Trial Chamber to transcript page 15461 and 15498. But most of them remained until May 6, 1992, and too many Croats remained for the accused. So his May 6 speech was designed to reach new dimensions of persecution by targeting Croats and sowing fear in the village. The events following the accused's persecution through his 6 May speech proves that he committed forcible transfer and deportation and that he aided and abetted and instigated others to persecute and forcibly transfer and deport Croats from Hrtkovci. Reports of his hate speech and the reaction of the crowd spread through the Croatian community of Hrtkovci. Fear and panic infected that community and news spread, as one would imagine, in a small village. It spread by word of mouth, from person to person, from household to household. And Croats decided they had no real choice but to leave Hrtkovci. The accused had warned them to "clear out of Serbia." And they did. They were so frightened after the speech, they started collecting travel documents and many left. The accused had directed Serbs to "promptly get rid of the remaining Croats in your and surrounding villages." They did. And they cleaned up the Croats who remained in Hrtkovci. The accused intended to and succeeded in instilling fear in the local Croat population against whom he advocated discrimination and violence. His speech aggravated an already tense situation between local Croats and Serb refugees in Hrtkovci. He created an atmosphere so coercive that most Croats could not remain there any longer. Local Croats took the accused's threats very seriously, and they took his threats very seriously because his hate speech was interpreted as that, a threat, a warning sign that simply "could not be ignored." After the speech, Croats began collecting travel documents. "They were standing in queues and waiting, like in embassies." And I'd direct the Trial Chamber to transcript page 9920, and direct the Trial Chamber to the evidence of Witnesses Paulic and VS-061 and VS-067 as well as Exhibits 555 and Exhibit P556. And the Trial Chamber heard evidence that Croats began collecting records - like c hristening certificates and marriage records - from the local Catholic church so that they could leave Hrtkovci. Requests for christening certificates and marriage records increased dramatically after the accused's hate speech. Witnesses testified that they left Hrtkovci as a direct result of the speech. So the accused lacks any credibility when he argues essentially that Croats exercised a genuine choice to leave Hrtkovci if they arranged house exchanges. Witness Ejic testified that nearly all those listed in the victim annex to the indictment, which he saw as Exhibit P558, he said: Nearly all of them "went to Croatia or even beyond." Transcript page 10407. He could only find two examples of people who left to Croatia of their own free will because, according to him, "everything else was done either out of fear or under different types of threat." Transcript page 10408. Croats did not choose to leave a community where they had been secure all their lives to go to the middle of a war in Croatia. They did not choose to uproot their lives, families, children, to leave their jobs and their friends, to go to a country being ravaged by a war they had been watching on television. They felt they had to leave because they thought their lives were in danger in Hrtkovci. For those Croats who remained, they remained because they were ready to die for staying there, and I direct the Trial Chamber's attention to Exhibit 555 on page 2. The demographic change underlying the renaming of Hrtkovci as Srbislavci is confirmed by the evidence of Witness Tabeau and the October 1992 report of the UN Special Rapporteu r, and this is Exhibit P982. And paragraph 22 of Exhibit P982 references the ethnic cleansing of Croats from Vojvodina. The demographic change is further corroborated by witness evidence and press articles memorialising the flight of Croats from Hrtkovci. And I've already listed one, Exhibit P555 and P556, just to list a few. Exhibit P555 is an article from "NIN" weekly and it's dated the 22nd of May, 1992, so two weeks after the accused's hate speech, and it's titled: "Hrtkovci - a village that is moving, Dr. Vojislav Seselj's programme to move out the non-Serb population from Serbia is becoming a reality." A retired local policeman explained in that article that: "It all began after Mr. Seselj's speech here in the village. Many people have already left the village." So all this evidence proves the impact of the accused's speech beyond a reasonable doubt. So when the accused claims that only eight people were forcibly displaced from Hrtkovci, it is an offensive and gross distortion of the facts. In his erroneous reading of the law, he argues that only those Croats who were physically harmed can qualify as being persecuted or forcibly displaced, and this is inconsistent with the law and the facts and should be rejected. The relevant paragraphs in the Prosecution closing brief can be found at 522, 529, 541, 550, and 555 to 564. I would like now to address the evidence that shows the accused aided, abetted, and instigated persecution and forcible transfer and deportation with his speech. His speech in Hrtkovci must be assessed in the context of all of his other language denigrating Croats. As one example, on April 1st, 1992, exactly as the Serb take-overs were being implemented in BiH, the accused used the National Assembly to attack Croats in Serbia. He said Croats should be forced from Serbia in retaliation for Tudjman forcing Serbs out of Croatia. He rejected the notion that there were any loyal Croats in Serbia, and this is reflected in Exhibit P16 which I will ask to be played now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Holding that the argument was not going in the right direction, Seselj asked to speak again. If the Croats are expelling the Serbs from Zagreb, what were the Croats waiting for in Belgrade and in Serbia? According to him, this represents a normal exchange of people in the principles of retortion or, as he explained it, retaliation. Mahmut Memic and Antun Skenderovic acted in response to this. Antun Skenderovic said that Seselj's viewpoints had already been known, but that it was good that that time he presented them from the Assembly floor and thus marked the Croats in Serbia as hostages. Further in his response, Seselj maintained that this regime was too lenient towards Croats and that after the next elections, all of them would be expelled and that not even those living in Serbia would sleep peacefully until they moved. "'By the same right Tudjman used to expel Serbs, we will expel Croats,' said Seselj, adding that he wanted to disperse another illusion about the loyal behaviour of Croats in Serbia, since, he maintained, 'They were aiding the Ustashas in this war too.'"

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So according to the accused, Croats were "aiding the Ustashas in this war too." And the accused maintained the pressure on Croats in Hrtkovci by making a special, personal appearance in that small village, mustering all the pomp and circumstance and political quasi-military trappings that had become the norm for his appearances. What resulted was a campaign of discrimination, coercion, and violence directed against Croats and some of the perpetrators are linked to the accused. Directly following the accused's May 6 speech, Croats were harassed, intimidated, and threatened in exactly the same way the accused had instructed in September of 1991. "Threats were coming in every day." Hand-grenades were thrown at Croat houses. Dogs were killed. Bomb threats were made. Transcript pages 10777, transcript page 9919, and Exhibits P551, P559, and P64 [sic], to name a few. The evidence shows that through his support and encouragement, the accused's tools, like Ostoja Sibincic, Rade Cakmak, and others, targeted Croats just as the accused intended with his May 6 speech. I refer the Trial Chamber to Exhibit P564, page 5; transcript pages 2471, 2475 to 2476; as well as Exhibits P1129, pages 26 to 28; and P1112, pages 5 to 6. Sibincic was one of the organisers of the May 6 SRS rally. He stood on the side of the stage during the speeches that day, and along with others, both he and Cakmak terrorised Croats in Hrtkovci. Both were the accused's men in Hrtkovci. In spring, they travelled to the SRS office in Belgrade where the accused gave him "the green light" to drive Croats from Hrtkovci. The accused had also given the green light to target -- to others to target Croats in Hrtkovci in May 1992. This evidence is reflected in Exhibits P1058, paragraphs 102 and 101; Exhibit P1056, paragraphs 87 to 88; Exhibit P1112, page 12; P1129, pages 27 to 28, and 65 to 66. Many inside and outside of Hrtkovci claimed that Sibincic worked closely with the accused, that he was the accused's right-hand man and that he did all the dirty work of the SRS in Hrtkovci. I refer the Chamber to the testimony of Witnesses Baricevic, Ejic, VS-067, VS-1036, VS-061, and P564, page 5. In August 1992, Sibincic and Cakmak were charged together with three others for committing crimes against Croats in Hrtkovci, but far from condemning their actions or even remaining silent, the accused on the 27th of August, 1992, publicly demanded their release. "Sibincic and the others arrested in Srbislavci, former Hrtkovci, should be immediately released." Exhibit P1202, page 10. And the accused is referring to Hrtkovci as former Hrtkovci mere months after his May 6 speech. With this public demand, the accused showed both his affiliation with Sibincic and he further encouraged and aided and abetted the criminal campaign of persecution and forcible displacement that had occurred in Hrtkovci. Before concluding, I will address some additional claims raised by the accused in his trial brief. First, the Trial Chamber had admitted the statement of Witness A on your sheet as P1112. His viva voce testimony was admitted as P1129. Witness A was cross-examined in that other case. His admitted evidence is credible and reliable. But the accused claims in his brief that Witness A is a Defence witness who recanted his OTP statements during another proceeding. One, I refer the Trial Chamber to the argumentative appendix to the Prosecution closing brief. Two, Witness A's unsworn, unadmitted statements are not evidence in this case. His sworn unadmitted testimony in another proceeding is not evidence in this case. What is in the trial record in this case as reliable and probative evidence are his admitted statement and admitted testimony. The second issue I'll address raised by the accused, according to him, he can only be convicted of instigating his followers or sympathisers if there had been a local SRS board in Hrtkovci at the time of the speech because that is the only manner in which he could have exerted any influence. This claim is baseless. There is no legal or factual basis for it and it should be rejected summarily. Even if it were true that the accused did not have a formal local board, he certainly had sympathisers and supporters - the very reason he could and did have a rally in Hrtkovci in the first place. And third, as set out in the Appeals Chamber decision on the 31st of August, 2004, in this case regarding the jurisdictional requirement, Article 5 does not require a material nexus between the acts of the accused and the armed conflict, only a connection between the Article 5 crime and the armed conflict. It is sufficient that the acts coincide geographically and temporally with the armed conflict. At all times relevant to the indictment, a state of armed conflict existed in Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the crimes committed by the accused in Hrtkovci are linked to the conflict in Croatia and to his pursuit of Greater Serbia. When the accused committed the crimes in Hrtkovci, a conflict was ongoing in Croatia. Both Serb and Croat civilians suffered the consequences of that conflict and Serbs from Croatia fled to Serbia. The Serb refugees who arrived in Hrtkovci saw Croats in Serbia as a cause of their suffering and tensions rose. And the accused himself makes the link between what was happening in Croatia and Serbia, and he charged Vojvodina Croats with conspiring with Tudjman as Ustashas. For example, on -- the Trial Chamber has other examples, but one example is from the 12th of June, 1992, when the accused declared in a radio interview that Croats "will have to move out according to the principles of reciprocity. I mean, since Tudjman expelled more than 300 [sic] Serbs, what are the Croats in Serbia waiting for?" 300.000 Serbs that should be, expelled more than 300 Serbs -- 300.000 Serbs. Furthermore, as the Trial Chamber has already heard, President Milosevic, president of the republic of Serbia, provided military, police, and political support from Serbia to the conflict in Croatia and BiH. The accused himself, he also gathered volunteers in Serbia and deployed them to Croatia and BiH. Consequently, the jurisdictional requirement under Article 5 is satisfied regarding Hrtkovci in Serbia, and this is highlighted in the Prosecution closing brief at paragraphs 542 to 544 and 548 to 550. The accused has not disputed the drastic demographic changes in Hrtkovci. What he offers are excuses and justifications seeking to disconnect himself from the mass exodus of Croats that his speech caused. None of these claimed justifications undermine the evidence presented by the Prosecution. In conclusion, the very fact that we can today speak of Hrtkovci before May 6, 1992, and after the accused's words on that day highlights how his crimes permanently changed the face of a peaceful multi-ethnic village in Serbia. I will conclude my remarks there, Your Honours, and then I will turn the lectern over to Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. [Interpretation] You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the accused's individual criminal responsibility for the crimes charged in the indictment has been proven beyond a reasonable doubt. For the accused, Greater Serbia is his raison d'etre. Throughout the trial, the accused has tried to cast himself as the victim of conspiracies and injustice because of an ideological belief in Greater Serbia. He makes these claims to distract attention from what the evidence in this case has proven; namely, that he is responsible for the suffering of tens of thousands of victims who were expelled from their homes, murdered, detained, tortured, raped, and whose villages, towns, and religious sites were wantonly destroyed as a result of his words and his acts. The disintegration of the former Yugoslavia tore its constituent republics apart. So the accused and other JCE members put aside their political differences, and the accused in close co-operation with other JCE members set out to create a Serb-only state. When the Serb autonomous regions were created in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, the accused began a relentless propaganda campaign to justify the creation of Greater Serbia. The accused's political position allowed him to deliver his propaganda to a wide audience. The same position cloaked his words with respectability. His propaganda was ethnically denigrating and dehumanising. He was a proponent of the idea that non-Serbs who once were neighbours, friends, and family were now subhuman, genocidal, and needed to be expelled from the new Greater Serbia by "all available means," as he said on the 5th of March 20 years ago. When he said non-Serbs should fear the Serbs, crimes targeting non-Serbs were soon committed. With his words, he planted the seeds of ethnic hatred and helped them grow into ethnic violence against non-Serbs. The accused crafted his public persona as the commander of an armed force that could carry out his will. Using the SCP and the SRS War Staff which he controlled, the accused recruited and organised thousands of volunteers. These volunteers were so closely associated with him that they were known as his men, Seseljevci. He sent them into Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina to support the newly created Serb structures such as TOs in Croatia and the SDS Crisis Staffs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. When the JNA as a result of desertion and the purging of non-Serbs was in need for his Seseljevci, he sent his units to participate in its operations in Croatia. His Seseljevci fought together with other Serb forces that the JNA members -- that the JCE members had established and controlled. Through his contacts with other JCE members and through his War Staff, the accused ensured that his Seseljevci were armed, equipped, transported, and deployed. He ensured that they had jobs to go back to and received benefits so they could be deployed. He provided encouragement and moral support with his visits to the front and in his speeches praising their successes. At least from August 1991, the joint Serb fighting force that the accused and other JCE members had created was engaged in a campaign of persecution against the non-Serb population in vast areas -- in vast areas of Croatia where the accused's Seseljevci became notorious for their brutality and crimes. Despite the horrible consequences of the campaign in Croatia, the accused continued his relentless propaganda campaign against Croats. He instigated the commission of further crimes by incessantly equating Croats to Ustasha fascists and he repeated his calls for blind revenge for Ustasha crimes against Serbs during the Second World War. As he intended, crimes were committed. The JNA wantonly destroyed Vukovar and forced most of its non-Serb population to flee. As they had done in area after area that had fallen before, when Vukovar fell, Serb forces, including numerous Seseljevci that the accused had personally decided to send to Vukovar, expelled, murdered, beat, tortured, raped, and abused the remaining non-Serb population. The accused and the other JCE members continued their persecutorial campaign in Bosnia and Herzegovina when it moved for independence. The accused fully supported the continued persecutorial campaign there. He intensified his propaganda campaign against Muslims and Croats. He sent thousands of his Seseljevci to support the newly established Crisis Staffs and TOs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The accused's threat of rivers of blood became gruesome reality for the non-Serbs when his Seseljevci in Bosnia and Herzegovina participated in the atrocities committed by Serb forces as they took control over Serb-claimed areas. In Zvornik, Greater Sarajevo, Mostar, and Nevesinje, his Seseljevci participated in the systematic expulsion, detention, murder, torture, rape, and other sexual abuse of non-Serbs and the wanton destruction of their property and religious sites. Your Honours, the evidence in this case has proven beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused is responsible for the commission of the crimes that he did not personally carry out, but which were committed by his Seseljevci and members of the Serb forces controlled by the JCE members set out in the indictment because, one, the accused and the other JCE members at least by August 1991 were joined in a common criminal purpose to conduct a widespread and systematic campaign of persecution against the non-Serbs in the areas targeted as Serb land in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Two, the crimes were an integral part of this common purpose. And three, the accused significantly contributed to the common criminal purpose by his relentless propaganda and instigation and by the thousands of Seseljevci that he sent to commit and participate in the crimes. The evidence has also proven that the accused committed persecution through hate speech in Vukovar and Hrtkovci. The speeches in these places threatened Croats and were given in the context of high ethnic tension. Those speeches beyond a reasonable doubt deprived the Croats in those areas of their right to safety and deprived them of their right to dignity. Moreover, as a result of the coercive environment that the accused created with his speech in Hrtkovci, as we have just heard, many Croats felt forced to leave the village. And he is therefore also responsible for deportation and forcible transfer. He is therefore guilty for the crimes set out in the indictment. And as set out in the Prosecution's closing brief, he is also responsible for instigating and aiding and abetting the crimes set out in the indictment. And now, proven guilty of these crimes, he must be punished. The accused's crimes in Vukovar, Zvornik, Greater Sarajevo, Mostar, Nevesinje, and Hrtkovci are grave, both in scale and by their heinous nature. His criminal acts and conduct dramatically changed the character of the targeted municipalities from multi-ethnic communities to Serb-only areas by forcibly transferring and deporting tens of thousands of non-Serbs, primarily Croats and Muslims; resulted in the devastation of towns and villages, including Croat and Muslim homes, hospitals, stores, and cemeteries; led to the plunder and encouraged the destruction of religious sites; and caused the murder of 905 people. Not only were the accused's crimes massive in scale, they were also particularly brutal. His acts and conduct contributed to the murder of children, newborns, pregnant women, the elderly, and the sick; crosses carved on the skin of Muslims; the rape of both women and men under the most sadistic of circumstances. His crimes deserve a punishment that reflects their gravity, and there are no mitigating circumstances. The accused's voluntarily surrender should not be considered a mitigating circumstance because it was his legal obligation to surrender. Moreover, in detention and in court his conduct have not warranted mitigation. On the contrary, the accused announced that he was here to "shatter the Tribunal" and he has used the trial as a political platform for his continued agenda of Serb ethnic supremacy. He has made every effort to obstruct the proper functioning of the Tribunal in its search for truth and accountability. The accused has been contemptuous throughout this trial. He persistently verbally abused witnesses in court despite repeated instructions from the Court to cease. He and his associates discouraged witnesses who were connected to the accused during the conflict from appearing and testifying truthfully, in some cases even instructing them on how to disavow their prior statements. And the accused has repeatedly breached orders for the protection of witnesses. These are significant aggravating circumstances. In addition, the accused shows no remorse. Of his propaganda and instigation, he has said before this Chamber, I quote: "And you think that what you were reading yesterday, the quotes from my speeches, and when you showed the clips of my speeches, that I was bothered. You did me a service. You have reminded the Serbian people of what I did over those years and how I gained my reputation amongst the Serbian people." He has also told the Tribunal repeatedly: "I am proud of everything I said then and I am prepared to repeat all of my speeches even today." And these two quotes are from transcript pages 16801 and 16818. And in fact, at the hearing on Monday he said about his words: These "are the words of a genius that I am still proud of even today." That is at transcript page 48, line 4, and I can provide the Chamber a bit later if needed with the transcript reference to the official transcript. No trial, conviction, and sentence will bring back the lives lost and ruined by the accused's crimes. But this fact just does not justify failing to impose a substantial sentence of imprisonment. The Prosecution recommends a sentence of 28 years to run consecutive to any other sentence imposed on him for his contempt of this Tribunal. That concludes the Prosecution's closing arguments for now. The Prosecution reserves its remaining time for arguments in rebuttal, should it become necessary, after the accused closing argument. I have two matters to just address to the Chamber. One is that I respectfully request that the pseudonym sheet that Ms. Biersay referred to in her submissions be added to the record as an exhibit marked for identification so that it is available for later review of the record. And the second thing is that at transcript page 17145, line 13, the name "Krajisnik" should have been "Karadzic." Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor. First of all, Registrar, regarding this document that has been given to us, we'd like to have an exhibit number for it, for us to be able to use it later on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit P1404, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The accused's closing arguments are scheduled to take place as of Monday at 2.15. He will have ten hours all included for his closing arguments. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber invites the accused, should he have any documents that he wants to use including the two books that he submitted to the Trial Chamber, one with a red cover, another with a blue cover, I'm not giving the titles, in order to make the interpreters' work easier. Just in case he might refer to pages in these two books, I invite him, therefore, to provide them prior to the Monday hearing through the Registrar so that the interpreters may prepare those pages he might want to use. These two books, the one with the blue cover, the other with the red cover, are new -- are re-prints. Therefore, there may be some changes between the latest book that we had and the one that we don't. So there may be inconsistencies or changes. So if he so wishes - of course he's not forced to - but if he can, he could provide these documents. This is not evidence, of course. These books are merely documents that he might want to refer to if he should feel the need to do so. Equally, when he makes his closing arguments, I should invite the Prosecution to remain silent unless there should be a mistake in the transcript or should the name of a protected witness be named. But of course, the Trial Chamber is free to make sure that doesn't happen. I repeat, closing arguments must be listened to in absolute silence, the same goes for the accused's closing arguments. Before I give the floor to Mr. Seselj -- yes, Mr. Marcussen, do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, as the Chamber just indicated, the books in question are not in evidence, so the Prosecution would find that it is improper for the accused to be referring to this. There might be certain excerpts of the books that are in evidence as separate Prosecution exhibits. And if the accused makes use of those, of course he's using the record and that is not a problem. But in our submission, he cannot be making reference to material which is not in evidence. He must confine himself to the trial record.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That interpretation is inaccurate. First of all, you stopped me from leading my Defence case. All the documents that I tendered during cross-examination at the beginning of the trial you refused. And after that, I stopped tendering anything, since you have not given me the possibility to lead my Defence case, I put forward to you in good time two of my books. One is "The Roman Catholic Project of the Creation of the Artificial Croatian Nation," and the other one is "The Ideology of Serbian Nationalism." I intend to use certain quotes from those books as an integral part of my closing arguments, not as leading evidence, because whatever I tendered you refused. You did not allow me to make my Defence case. For me, that is over. But instead of recalling things off the top of my head, I intend to read passages from those books. I will not provide those quotes in advance. The translation service can make copies of these books and when I say page so and so, they can find the page. I don't have the ability to provide this. I have no one to help me and the administration of the prison does not allow me to make any submissions because they don't want to make photocopies for me, and photocopies are the only proof I have of submitting something. The reason I wanted the floor is to say this. Mr. Marcussen does not have the right to reserve time. He was granted ten hours for the Prosecution's closing arguments. He didn't know how to use all of the ten hours; that's his problem. I will use all of my ten hours, and I may ask for another two or three hours in addition; that's my right. In all the other cases where the accused is self-represented, he is given advantages in terms of time. For instance, Mr. Milosevic had 60 per cent as opposed to 40 per cent of the Prosecution. In other cases, the accused's time is not limited. You have limited me to the time used by the Prosecution. I will probably - although I don't know yet, I can't estimate properly now - I may well ask for additional time. The Prosecution has the right to a rebuttal. You will decide how much time. But it's not the time that he has spared. Whatever time you give the Prosecutor for rebuttal, you will have to give me the same amount of time to respond to the rebuttal; that's my right. I will not reserve any time from my closing argument and I'm just reminding you that you have to do this. And if you don't do it, even better for me. That's another argument how this Tribunal is humiliating itself. And I prefer to see you losing face --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... decision the Trial Chamber has set the amount of hours for each party and made sure to say that closing arguments for either party are but an addition to the briefs that were filed. The Prosecution filed their briefs, so did you. Yours are over 600 pages long. We were infinitely generous towards you and we granted you ten hours, which is an inordinate amount of time. I have no memory in this Tribunal of closing arguments lasting as many as ten hours. Usually much less time is given for the purpose. However, this Tribunal says that in exceptional circumstances following closing arguments the practice is that the Prosecutor may have the floor for specific points, in which case the Defence is also entitled obviously to close the proceedings in speaking last. This is the rule in law on this matter. Closing arguments are closing arguments. You've heard the Prosecution's closing arguments. You're now totally free to speak to whatever topic you decide, but please do not waste the Trial Chamber's time. We therefore will make sure that your time is used in the best way possible for your Defence. But I'm not worried, I'm sure that you're going to make best use of your time. You told us that despite my invitation to give the books to the interpreters, you have decided not to do so. Well, interpreters are wonderful anyway -- make wonders. And I've read the two books, so of course I'll make sure that I can check what you say because I have read over 2.000 pages in preparation for this. And you yourself admitted that this is not in evidence or evidence, but that you will refer to these books. So I see no problem whatsoever. Yes, Mr. Seselj, one last word.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I no longer have the books in English. My legal advisors recently brought me five sets of those books, and immediately, as soon as they entered the prison building, I handed them over to the guards to forward to the Tribunal; three sets for the Trial Chamber, one set for the Prosecutor, and one set for the Registrar. I don't see that I could have done anything more. They could not have brought more than that. And it turns out that their visit, since I was not given the right to privileged communication, we spent two days sitting down talking about anything. We couldn't talk about my case because the conversation was eavesdropped. My Case Manager Nemanja Sarovic was present but we could not have access to privileged communication. Since we didn't have an interpreter to control our conversation, we concluded that the conversation was eavesdropped, and they had the right to do that because at the outset they told us that our communication was not privileged. They brought five sets of books. If they had sent them by mail or if my wife had brought them to the prison, the prison officers would have provided me with just one set and the rest would have been confiscated. Nobody would have ever asked me why I needed five sets because the prison authorities are afraid of my propaganda being spread amongst other detainees. One thing more I need to tell you. I learned yesterday from a document that I had been provided by the Registry was -- that there was a ban on my contacting all the other prisoners, and that was never provided in writing to me. We're talking about Goran Hadzic and some others. Why do I know that that applies to Goran Hadzic? Because Hadzic was in the living room with his family and I was locked up with my legal advisors. This is just unheard of. If there is any reason for that communication to be banned, then I should be provided with an order and an explanation. Why Hadzic of all people? Because in my proceedings I unmasked everything that was happening around Ovcara, and the Prosecution is still insisting on the old story about the military security service, the civilian security service, everybody handing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I was saying that the Trial Chamber hasn't banned anything whatsoever and the issue you are raising comes under the competence of the President and the Registry, not us. So what you have just said is on the transcript, but as far as we are concerned, I can confirm that we haven't banned anything whatsoever. That said, since everything has been said, we shall meet again at a quarter past 2.00 on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
